title: The saw, alone
tomorrow: two extremes, one middle. what did he tell his five old friends?

lines: A COMMENT, AND YOUR CHEST IS A FIST.
A HOE AGAINST THE WHOLE EARTH.
cards: Press your palm flat against the floor for a second. Solid. It doesn't flinch when someone walks on it, or drops a bag, or spills a drink.
Now the opposite: a comment under your post, a remark in class, and suddenly your whole chest is a fist. MN 21, read straight through, answers with that floor.
Someone takes a hoe and a basket and says, i'll make this great earth not be earth. He digs and scatters and digs. Can he do it?

teach.h: THE EARTH IS TOO DEEP TO DIG AWAY.
teach.b: No, the sutta says. The earth is deep and vast; he'll only wear himself out. Then the Buddha turns it toward speech.

teach.h: FIVE WAYS PEOPLE SPEAK TO YOU.
teach.b: People will talk to you in five ways, he says, in paraphrase: at the right time or the wrong time, truly or falsely, gently or harshly, to help or to harm, with goodwill or with hate.
Whatever they choose, train like this: my mind stays unshaken, no harsh word comes out of me, i keep goodwill toward them, and i fill the world with a mind like the earth, wide, without hostility.

teach.h: PAINT ON SPACE. BURN A RIVER.
teach.b: Try to paint pictures on empty space with dye: nothing sticks. Try to burn a great river with a grass torch: it won't catch. Stroke a soft, tanned catskin bag with your hand: it doesn't crackle.

teach.h: THE SAW: HATE ISN'T THE TEACHING.
teach.b: And the sutta's name comes from its hardest image, which younger listeners can skip past: even if bandits cut you with a saw, a mind that turns to hate isn't following the teaching.
The point isn't to stay where you're hurt.
It's that their words don't get to decide what your mind becomes.

how: The simile of the saw is taught in Buddhist communities as a standard for patience (khanti) and goodwill; some practitioners recall the earth simile when they're criticized.

o: a rule against monks owning sharp objects
a tool monks used to cut wood for their huts
MN 21's picture for keeping goodwill under any attack

games.q: the pictures in MN 21 — tap the pairs.
p: too deep and vast to dig away
a grass torch on a river

s: MN 21 tells you to stay wherever you're being hurt
its training is about your mind and your words: no hate, no harsh reply. it doesn't tell anyone to stay in harm's way.
the sutta lists ways people may speak to you, kind and unkind
timely or not, true or false, gentle or harsh, helpful or not, with goodwill or hate.
a mind like the earth means feeling nothing at all
the earth still gets dug at; it just doesn't stop being earth. goodwill stays.

games.q: someone in the group chat mocks your new haircut. you've already felt the sting. what does MN 21 point to?
o: let it land without handing hate back, and keep goodwill
post the sharpest comeback you can write
act like it didn't hurt and leave the chat for good
games.why: the sutta doesn't ask you not to feel it. it asks that no harsh word come out of you and that goodwill stay, like earth that's dug at and still earth.

practice: Put both palms on the floor or the ground beside you, and keep them there the whole sit. Feel how it holds your weight without pushing back.
Bring to mind one sharp thing someone said, let it land, and feel the ground under your hands stay just as it is. If you can, end by wishing that person well, once.

wordCard.voice: The saw: MN 21, the simile of the saw, on keeping goodwill even when words, or worse, come at you.

orig.note: Pali: saw. MN 21 is the Kakacupama Sutta, the simile of the saw.

carryVoice: A mind like the earth: dig all you like, it stays earth. Sutta three, read alone.
